title: The wall that met the tiger
hookLine: a yogi rides in on a tiger, and the children ride out on a wall
carry: siddhis aren't holiness; the saint prays for all

cards: Here comes a yogi, riding a tiger. In his hand, instead of a whip, a live snake. Behind him, a crowd of disciples.
His name is Changdev, and tradition remembers him as a man of great yogic powers. He's heard about a young saint at Alandi, and he's coming to see him.
At the other end of the road, Jnaneshwar, his brothers and his sister are sitting on a low wall in the sun. Someone runs up: he's coming.

teach.b: It starts with a letter that was never written. Changdev couldn't decide how to address Jnaneshwar. As an equal?
A teacher? A boy? So he sent a blank sheet.
Muktabai, the sister, is said to have read it and remarked that all his years of practice had left him blank. Then the tiger, the snake, the crowd. Jnaneshwar doesn't climb down.
The story says he asks the wall to move, and the wall carries the four children down the road. Changdev, who had mastered a living tiger, sees children riding on stone, and the pride goes out of him.
Tradition says he became a disciple, some tellings say of Muktabai herself. Here's the teaching under the joke. Hindu tradition has a word for powers like taming tigers: siddhis.
The Yoga Sutras warn that such powers are obstacles on the way to samadhi. Stories like this one say it plainly: power isn't holiness. What holiness looks like comes at the close of the Jnaneshwari.
Jnaneshwar asks God for a gift, a pasayadan, and it isn't for himself.
He asks that the crookedness of the wicked fall away, that they come to love doing good, and that all beings become friends to one another.
Tradition says that later, at Alandi, still a young man, he entered samadhi, a final meditation.

teach.h: THE PASAYADAN: A GIFT FOR ALL.
teach.b: So today, when you feel the pull to arrive on a tiger, at the temple or anywhere, the saint points to a plainer thing: humility, and a prayer that includes everyone.

how: Marathi-speaking devotees often recite the Pasayadan at the close of worship or gatherings, and pilgrims visit Jnaneshwar's samadhi shrine at Alandi, where his palanquin sets out on the Varkari pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

s: the saints treat yogic powers as proof of holiness
the Yoga Sutras call such powers obstacles, and a willing wall humbled the tiger rider.
Changdev sent a blank letter ahead
he couldn't decide how to address Jnaneshwar.
in the Pasayadan, Jnaneshwar asks for his own fame
he asks for the crookedness of the wicked to fall away and for all beings to be friends.

games.q: you're Jnaneshwar, sitting on a wall with your brothers and sister. a well-known yogi is coming, riding a tiger. what do you do?
o: climb down and walk out to meet him.
ask the wall to carry you.
send him a blank letter of your own.
games.why: the story says the wall moves and carries the four children, and Changdev's pride falls away: his powers, his siddhis, were never holiness.

practice: Marathi-speaking devotees often close worship with the Pasayadan. Sit as you are, the way the children sat on the wall. Notice any wish to arrive impressively today, and let it soften.
Then pray the way the Pasayadan does, for everyone: may the crookedness in people fall away; may all beings be friends. Wish it for the people you'll see, even one who's been hard on you.
If you don't pray, simply wish each of them well, one by one.

wordCard.voice: Jnaneshwar. The Marathi saint who rode a willing wall to meet a yogi on a tiger, and closed his book asking good for all beings.

orig.note: Marathi, in Devanagari: the gift Jnaneshwar asks of God at the end of his book.
